bibliographic.title: The Use of Chatbots in Oncological Care: A Narrative Review
bibliographic.authors: Alexander Wang, Zhiyu Qian, Logan Briggs, Alexander P Cole, Leonardo O Reis, Quoc-Dien Trinh
bibliographic.citation_apa: Wang, A., Qian, Z., Briggs, L., Cole, A. P., Reis, L. O., & Trinh, Q.-D. (2023). The use of chatbots in oncological care: A narrative review. International Journal of General Medicine. https://doi.org/10.2147/IJGM.S408208

methodology.study_design: PubMed literature search with narrative synthesis
methodology.sample_description: Studies investigating chatbot use in any aspect of oncological care (prevention, patient education, treatment, surveillance)
methodology.technology_context: Chatbots and conversational agents using natural language processing, machine learning, and broader artificial intelligence; includes voice-based platforms such as Siri and Watson; no large language models explicitly discussed

eligibility.decision_rationale: Narrative review clearly addresses chatbots and conversational agents in oncological care within a regulated healthcare domain, but the provided text focuses on applications, satisfaction, efficacy, and implementation limitations rather than conversational governance, accountability, guardrails, audit, or LLM-specific systems.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Confirm whether later sections discuss bias, transparency, compliance, human oversight, or LLM-based chatbots beyond the excerpts supplied; triage flagged governance terms not visible in provided text.

appraisal.notes: Search strategy and inclusion criteria are stated, but as a narrative review with PubMed-only retrieval through April 2022, synthesis rigor and governance-related appraisal are limited in the supplied text.

cerqual.explanation: The review coherently summarizes oncological chatbot applications and outcomes, but its relevance to conversational governance and LLM-based systems is indirect; narrative design and single-database scope limit confidence for governance-focused synthesis.

coding.theme: Clinical deployment of chatbots in oncological care

synthesis.main_claim: Chatbots in oncological care show high user satisfaction and frequent efficacy in improving communication and access to cancer-related information, but widespread implementation is limited by the need for extensive user-testing and iterative improvement.
synthesis.contribution: Provides a domain-specific map of oncological chatbot applications across prevention, education, treatment, and surveillance, synthesizing 21 included studies.
synthesis.limitations: Narrative review scope; PubMed-only search through April 2022; limited discussion of governance, safety, compliance, or LLM architectures in the provided text.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational contextual evidence for regulated healthcare chatbot applications and implementation barriers; not central evidence for conversational governance frameworks or LLM-specific governance mechanisms.

evidence.claim: Study is a narrative review of chatbots in oncological care
evidence.excerpt: The Use of Chatbots in Oncological Care: A Narrative Review
The initial search yielded 196 records, 21 of which met inclusion criteria.

evidence.claim: Inclusion focused on chatbot use across oncological care phases
evidence.excerpt: Inclusion criteria were chatbot use in any aspect of oncological care—prevention, patient education, treatment, and surveillance.

evidence.claim: Chatbots are defined via NLP-based conversational simulation
evidence.excerpt: Chatbots are defined as computer programs that process and simulate human conversation by artificially replicating patterns of human interaction through natural language processing.

evidence.claim: Technology context includes AI and machine learning, not LLMs
evidence.excerpt: With advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning technology, increasing efforts have been made to use chatbots to automate specific aspects of oncological care.

evidence.claim: Regulated healthcare domain is oncology/cancer care
evidence.excerpt: We aimed to assess the current applications, limitations, and challenges in the literature on chatbots employed in oncological care.

evidence.claim: Reported applications include screening, prevention, monitoring, and management
evidence.excerpt: The most reported chatbot applications were cancer screening, prevention, risk stratification, treatment, monitoring, and management.

evidence.claim: High satisfaction and efficacy reported in included studies
evidence.excerpt: Good patient satisfaction was reported among 14 of 21 chatbots.

evidence.claim: Implementation limited by user-testing and iterative improvement needs
evidence.excerpt: Currently, chatbots are primarily limited by the need for extensive user-testing and iterative improvement before widespread implementation.

evidence.claim: Mixed chatbot performance example with low satisfaction
evidence.excerpt: the chatbot only had an average satisfaction rating of 54%, adherence was low, and no improvement was seen in knowledge of lung cancer symptom management.
